query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy during elevated-temperature exposure is governed primarily by the synergistic oxidation of Cr and Ti. In oxidizing atmospheres, these elements rapidly form a continuous, mixed Cr/Ti oxide layer that protects the underlying fcc matrix, whereas in reducing atmospheres the suppressed oxidation leads to insufficient external oxide formation, resulting in enhanced internal oxidation and localized matrix degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐manufactured, homogeneous fcc-phase Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with minimal pre-existing oxide, retaining high strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Expose identical sample sets to controlled high-temperature conditions in two distinct atmospheres: one oxidizing (e.g., air) and one reducing (e.g., a hydrogen-containing environment) at analogous temperatures.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900°C) for durations sufficient to develop measurable oxide scales (e.g., 50 hours), with a precise control of the oxygen partial pressure in the oxidizing tests and hydrogen partial pressure in the reducing tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The diffusion kinetics of Cr and Ti within the fcc matrix and their subsequent segregation to the surface or internal grain boundaries mediate oxidative scale formation and internal oxidation pathways.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, Cr and Ti preferentially oxidize to form a continuous, adherent mixed oxide scale that acts as a barrier against further degradation while preserving the matrix integrity. In contrast, under reducing conditions, the inhibited oxidation process prevents the formation of this protective layer, leading to elemental depletion near the surface and promoting internal oxidation and microstructural degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: In oxidizing atmospheres, the alloy will develop a well‐defined Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale that protects the fcc matrix, maintaining mechanical integrity. In reducing atmospheres, observable internal oxidation, such as depletion zones near grain boundaries or within the matrix, will emerge, correlating with a reduction in localized material properties.
generation.baseline: The starting state is the as‐manufactured alloy with a uniform fcc matrix, proven strength and fatigue properties, and little to no significant oxidation prior to testing.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected within the tested temperature range (700–900°C) and exposure durations (around 50 hours); outside these limits, additional phase transformations or degradation modes might dominate and confound the observed effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance and kinetics of Cr and Ti oxidation under varied reducing conditions remain uncertain, as do the potential influences of subtle additive manufacturing–induced microstructural variations on oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in-situ high-temperature oxidation/corrosion experiments on identical alloy samples exposed under tightly controlled oxidizing (air) and reducing (H2-containing) atmospheres at 800°C for 50 hours. Utilize surface characterization methods (e.g., XPS, SEM-EDS) to quantify the composition and continuity of the oxide scale and cross-sectional TEM imaging to assess depth and distribution of internal oxidation. Complement these with mechanical property evaluations (e.g., hardness, fatigue tests) after exposure to correlate microstructural changes with degradation.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and continuity (XPS, SEM-EDS)
Internal oxidation depth and location (cross-sectional TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if (a) in oxidizing conditions, the oxide scale is not enriched in Cr and Ti or does not form a continuous, protective layer, or (b) if reducing conditions yield no significant differences in internal oxidation (i.e., similar protective scales and microstructural integrity as observed under oxidizing conditions), thereby refuting the predicted mechanism of atmosphere-dependent degradation.

chosen.approach: In‐situ oxidation/corrosion characterization of high‐entropy alloys
